title: A Confession for the Ledger
premise: Retired detective Emrys Eriksen buried his old partner, Halloran, and thought the past was finally closed—until a confession letter arrives, postmarked the day after the funeral, naming Emrys as an accessory to a murder thirty years cold. The letter points to a ledger hidden in plain sight among the bookshop's stock, one that records every favor, bribe, and body that built their careers. As Emrys decodes it, he realizes someone else is hunting the ledger too: the surviving beneficiary of the old cover-up, who will burn the shop—and Emrys—to keep it buried. In the end, Emrys must choose between destroying the evidence to protect his fragile new life or surrendering it to give a forgotten victim's family the truth, choosing truth at the cost of everything he built to stay invisible.
about_author: Jonah Reyes is a former small-town newspaper reporter who spent a decade covering cold cases before turning to fiction full-time. He writes from a cluttered apartment above a used bookstore, where he claims half his plots arrive in other people's returned paperbacks.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Emrys Eriksen, three weeks into retirement and drowning in unsold stock at his failing bookshop, opens mail addressed in his dead partner's handwriting. The letter confesses to a murder and names Emrys. His POV; the beat is dread disguised as routine—the past knocking on glass he thought was soundproof.

chapters.title: The Funeral That Wasn't Over
chapters.summary: Emrys checks the postmark: dated the day after Halloran's funeral. He replays the funeral, noticing who attended and who didn't—including a woman in gray no one claimed. Flashbacks establish his partnership with Halloran. Emotional beat: grief curdling into suspicion that even mourning was staged.

chapters.title: Inventory of Ghosts
chapters.summary: The letter references 'the ledger, where you always kept it.' Emrys begins searching his own inventory, realizing Halloran knew his cataloging system intimately. POV shifts briefly to the woman in gray watching the shop. Beat: paranoia takes root; home becomes a crime scene of memory.

chapters.title: Thirty Years Cold
chapters.summary: Emrys digs out his private case notes from 1994: the disappearance of a young accountant, Mara Voss, ruled a runaway. The confession letter describes her death in detail only the killer would know. Beat: guilt surfaces—he helped bury the case without questioning why.

chapters.title: A Customer Who Doesn't Read
chapters.summary: A well-dressed man buys nothing but asks pointed questions about rare acquisitions and Emrys's 'retirement.' Emrys recognizes the manner of Internal Affairs. His POV; beat: the hunter realizes he is also hunted, and the statute clock becomes tangible.

chapters.title: Where You Always Kept It
chapters.summary: Emrys decodes the letter's second page—a cipher keyed to Dewey decimal numbers matching shelf locations. First fragment found inside a hollowed-out atlas: columns of initials, dates, payments. Beat: grim awe; Halloran turned corruption into bookkeeping, and Emrys can read every line.

chapters.title: The Woman in Gray
chapters.summary: She introduces herself as Nadia Voss, Mara's sister, still searching after thirty years. She suspects Emrys knows something. Her POV chapter reveals she received an anonymous tip—the same week Halloran died. Beat: uneasy alliance forming over shared suspicion of the same dead man.

chapters.title: Entries and Omissions
chapters.summary: Emrys cross-references ledger fragments against old cases, finding a pattern: every entry conceals a payoff, and one recurring initial—'R.K.'—collected more than anyone. He realizes R.K. is alive, powerful, and positioned to destroy him. Beat: the price of survival made arithmetic.

chapters.title: Fire Inspection
chapters.summary: An official inspection threatens the shop with closure—timed too perfectly to be coincidence. Emrys hides the recovered fragments off-site. Beat: siege mentality; the enemy is closing in through paperwork instead of bullets, which frightens him more.

chapters.title: What Halloran Kept From Me
chapters.summary: Emrys visits Halloran's widow, who hands over a locked box Halloran left 'for when Emrys comes asking.' Inside: photographs of Mara Voss alive, taken weeks after her supposed death date. Beat: vertigo—the confession may be a lie, or the timeline itself was forged.

chapters.title: Two Confessions
chapters.summary: Comparing the letter with the box contents, Emrys finds contradictions suggesting two different authors. Someone forged Halloran's hand—or Halloran wrote two versions for two audiences. Beat: betrayal deepens; even his partner's last words were a manipulation.

chapters.title: Nadia's Ledger
chapters.summary: Nadia shares her own decades of research—clippings, interviews, a list of everyone who profited from Mara's erasure. Their lists overlap with R.K.'s entries. Beat: belonging; two lonely investigators recognize each other, and the hunt becomes shared rather than solitary.

chapters.title: The Middle Shelf
chapters.summary: Decoding the final cipher key hidden in a first edition Halloran gave Emrys years ago, they locate the complete ledger concealed in the shop's false wall. Beat: triumph shadowed by terror—they now hold the thing everyone is willing to kill for.

chapters.title: R.K., Revealed
chapters.summary: The ledger's largest beneficiary is Raymond Kessler, now a judge—and the man who signed off on closing Mara's case. Emrys remembers Kessler as a young detective who owed them favors. Beat: the machinery of the old cover-up snaps into focus, terrifyingly ordinary.

chapters.title: Offer on the Table
chapters.summary: Kessler visits the shop personally: pension protection, quiet money, the letter's origin never questioned—in exchange for the ledger. Emrys stalls. Beat: temptation rendered honestly; invisibility and comfort are offered back if he'll just stop looking.

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: The shop's back room catches fire overnight—arson disguised as faulty wiring. Emrys saves what matters and realizes Kessler won't negotiate twice. Nadia urges going public; Emrys hesitates, knowing exposure ends his life as constructed. Beat: rock bottom; the price of survival comes due.

chapters.title: The Forger's Hand
chapters.summary: Examining the confession letter under magnification, Emrys identifies the tremor pattern—it was written by someone dying, copying Halloran's samples. Not Halloran's hand at all: someone wanted the ledger found. Beat: reversal; the confession was bait, and Emrys must find who cast it.

chapters.title: Halloran's Last Case
chapters.summary: Following the forgery thread, Emrys reconstructs Halloran's final months: the old man had grown conscience-stricken, planned to expose Kessler, and died suspiciously fast of 'heart failure.' Beat: grief recontextualized—his partner's death may be the story's true murder.

chapters.title: Statute Midnight
chapters.summary: With days before the civil claim expires, Emrys and Nadia deliver copies of the ledger to a journalist, the state attorney, and Mara's remaining family—simultaneously, so it cannot be quietly swallowed. Beat: resolve; Emrys chooses truth over the invisible life.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Stacks
chapters.summary: Kessler comes for the original ledger himself. In the ruined shop, Emrys uses thirty years of detective craft—not force—to trap Kessler into recorded admissions while Nadia witnesses. Beat: climax; the retired detective's skills, once complicit tools, become instruments of reckoning.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Kessler is arrested; Halloran's death reopened; the ledger entered into evidence. Emrys testifies, confessing his own small betrayals publicly. Beat: catharsis through accountability—survival's price paid in full, willingly, in daylight.

chapters.title: Open for Business
chapters.summary: Months later, the rebuilt shop reopens with a memorial shelf for Mara Voss and a plaque for Halloran. Nadia stays in town; Emrys, no longer hiding, greets customers by name. Final beat: belonging earned—the visible life, chosen at last, is the one worth keeping.
